title: What are manufacturers actually using AI for?
description: AI in manufacturing for a 40-500 person plant: where it pays first, tool prices, the rules that apply and what employers hire for.
verdict: Fix maintenance first. The most reactive quarter of plants had 3.3x the downtime and 16x the defects of the least.[^1][^2]
Start with a troubleshooting assistant reading manuals and repair history, no new sensors needed.[^4] One plant cut repair time 40%.[^3]
Trained inspectors caught just 85% of bad parts.[^6] Most published camera AI stalls at pilot, so test on your parts.[^7]
Expect a dip before the gain. Productivity falls first after AI adoption; plants that drop structured management lose more.[^8][^9]
People keep the switch. Federal guidance keeps humans in the loop on machine-control AI,[^10] and OSHA lockout rules cover repairs.[^11]

onPage.text: Where AI pays first in a plant, ranked by payoff and effort
What plants search for, and what employers hire for, from our own count
What maintenance and inspection tools cost
The safety, FDA and defense rules that apply
How plant AI projects go wrong, and the fix for each
Buy or build, and when to pick something else

headings.ranked: Where does AI pay first in a plant?
headings.buy-or-build: Should you buy AI tools or build your own?
headings.faq: Questions plant leaders ask about AI

summary: AI in manufacturing reads data your plant already makes, such as machine signals, camera images and manuals, to flag failing machines and catch defects.[^13][^4] What changes: technicians fix machines faster; one plant's AI assistant cut repair time and downtime 40%.[^3] People still decide what to fix, ship or scrap.[^10]
humanRole: Operators and the maintenance lead keep control of the machines. Federal and allied guidance urges caution with AI that acts on machine control, and wants human checkpoints.[^10][^12]
The maintenance planner owns the work order; AI only raises the flag. A trained person still locks out the machine's power under OSHA rules before any AI-suggested repair.[^11][^10]
The quality manager decides what ships, reworks or gets scrapped; the camera only sorts and flags. Medical-device makers must also show that this software works, under FDA rules.[^16][^17]
Technicians still do the fix, and AI answers their questions faster. In one McKinsey case, technicians gained 40% more capacity because they rarely had to answer simple questions.[^4][^18]

ranked.name: A troubleshooting assistant for maintenance
ranked.why: Lowest effort: it reads the manuals and repair notes you already have, with no new sensors.[^4] One plant built its assistant in two weeks and cut repair time 40%.[^3]
ranked.payoff: Mean time to repair, and the share of calls operators solve without a technician.

ranked.name: Predictive maintenance on the few machines that stop the line
ranked.why: The average US plant still does 45.7% of its maintenance after something breaks.[^1][^2] Plants leaning on planned and predictive work had 52.7% less unplanned downtime.[^19]
ranked.payoff: Unplanned downtime hours on the covered machines, and your share of reactive maintenance hours.

ranked.name: AI camera inspection on one defect that reaches customers
ranked.why: Half of 1,560 manufacturers planned AI for quality in 2025, the top use case.[^5] Trained inspectors caught 85% of bad parts and wrongly rejected 35% of good ones.[^6]
ranked.payoff: Escapes to customers per quarter, false rejects, and inspection minutes per part.

ranked.name: Reading quotes, orders and certificates
ranked.why: Language models fit the paperwork around the plant, like requests for quote and supplier contracts.[^52][^53] GE Appliances says a supplier-email agent helped cut backorders 25% (Google's claim).[^21]
ranked.payoff: Hours from request for quote to quote sent, and keying errors per 100 documents.

ranked.name: Production scheduling and process optimization
ranked.why: This is where employers hire: we counted 2,535 US ads for process optimization and 1,607 for scheduling optimization in one week.[^22][^23] It needs clean routings plus production and supply data from your ERP (business system).[^13]
ranked.payoff: On-time delivery, schedule changes per week, and scrap or yield percentage.

ranked.name: Energy use and digital twins
ranked.why: Save these for later: they need the most data plumbing. Energy AI drew almost no US searches in our pull, though 290 job ads mentioned it in a week.[^24][^22]

ownData.title: What do plants search for, and what do employers hire for?
ownData.intro: US plants search most for predictive maintenance, while US job ads name process optimization and production scheduling most.[^24][^22] We set US Google searches for each kind of manufacturing AI work against US job ads that mention it.[^24][^22] The Federal Reserve sees the same pull: about 11% of manufacturing job postings asked for AI skills in 2026, against about 8% overall.[^23]
ownData.note: Searches are US Google monthly averages for three phrases per row, from our keyword pull of 25 Nov 2026.[^24] Job ads are US ads posted in the 7 days to 25 Nov 2026 that mention the row's phrase.[^22] Counts are rough: ads aren't limited to manufacturers, and one ad can match several rows.

rules.name: OSHA lockout/tagout, 29 CFR 1910.147
rules.what: Covers servicing any machine that could start up unexpectedly and hurt someone.[^11] An AI maintenance alert doesn't change who locks out the power. It was OSHA's 4th most-cited standard in FY2025, with 2,177 violations.[^29][^30]

rules.name: OSHA machine guarding, 29 CFR 1910.212
rules.what: Keep guards in place when you add cameras or robots for AI inspection. It was OSHA's 10th most-cited standard in FY2025, with 1,239 violations.[^29]

rules.name: ISO 10218-1 and 10218-2:2025, robot safety
rules.what: The baseline for any AI-guided robot or cobot cell. It replaces the 2011 edition and is a paid standard.[^31]

rules.name: FDA QMSR, 21 CFR 820 (medical devices)
rules.what: It folds in ISO 13485:2016 and now specifically requires risk management.[^16] AI used in production or quality falls inside your quality system.[^17]

rules.name: FDA Computer Software Assurance guidance
rules.what: A risk-based way to show that software used in production or quality does its job.[^17] Treat AI tools in those steps the same way.

rules.name: CMMC, DFARS rule (defense suppliers)
rules.what: If you handle controlled unclassified information (CUI), any cloud AI tool that touches it must sit inside your assessed environment.[^32] Full rollout comes on 10 Nov 2028.[^33]

rules.name: EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230
rules.what: Only if you sell machines into the EU. It replaces the Machinery Directive and was amended in 2026 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.[^34]

rules.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
rules.what: A free framework for naming who oversees AI and how you check it. It puts risks of serious injury or death first.[^12]

rules.name: CISA and allies, AI in operational technology
rules.what: Ask vendors for a software bill of materials (SBOM) that covers embedded AI. Get data-use terms so the vendor may not train on your plant data.[^10]

rules.name: NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3, OT security
rules.what: The US reference for securing the systems that run your machines (OT) before you connect AI to them.[^35]

watchOuts: Pilot purgatory: 77% of AI vision systems in a 50-study review never left prototype or pilot.[^7][^36] Cost the problem first, in downtime hours or escapes, and start on one line.[^14][^37]
Productivity dips before it rises, worst in older plants.[^8][^9] Budget a ramp period and keep your standard work, since dropping it explains about a third of the losses.[^8]

Alert fatigue: NIST MEP warns that even a 2% false-alarm rate can mean dozens of false alarms a day, until staff ignore alarms entirely.[^13] Fix basic preventive maintenance first, then set alert limits with the technicians who act on them.

Vision models drift when lighting, material or product changes, and lab accuracy overstates the line.[^36][^7] Trial on your own parts, keep every labelled image and budget for upkeep, since plant AI is never a one-time fix.[^13]

Connecting machines opens a cyber door: manufacturing was the most-attacked industry for the fifth year running, per IBM.[^38][^39] Follow NIST SP 800-82 and the CISA AI-in-OT principles before you connect.[^35][^10]

Lock-in: NIST MEP warns that big tech is easy to get into and hard to get out of.[^14] Get data-use terms in writing and prefer open standards such as MTConnect, so you can export your own data.[^10][^40]

faq.q: Is predictive maintenance worth it, or mostly a sales pitch?
faq.a: Predictive maintenance is often worth it, but only once basic preventive work is in place. NIST found the less reactive half of plants had 52.7% less unplanned downtime.[^19] The Department of Energy puts predictive savings at 8% to 12% over preventive work, but it needs diagnostic gear and training.[^47]

faq.q: What is the difference between predictive and preventive maintenance?
faq.a: Preventive maintenance runs on a calendar or cycle count, while predictive maintenance is triggered by measured condition, such as vibration or temperature.[^1][^2] NIST found predictive-heavy plants had 18.5% less unplanned downtime than preventive-heavy ones.[^19]

faq.q: Does predictive maintenance only work for big companies?
faq.a: No, small plants can use predictive maintenance too, starting with one troubled machine. The Department of Energy says to fix one troubled system first and leave cheap, unimportant equipment to reactive repair.[^47] Maintenance software runs $20 to $75 per user a month,[^25][^26] while sensor systems are quoted per site.[^50][^49]

faq.q: How much does AI visual inspection cost?
faq.a: AI visual inspection costs $0 on a free tier and up to six figures for a custom system.[^28][^13] NIST MEP puts simple industrial AI setups at a few thousand dollars and custom ones at hundreds of thousands.[^13] The LandingLens free model download is for non-commercial use only.[^28]

faq.q: How many manufacturers actually use AI?
faq.a: Fewer than the hype suggests: about 12% of US manufacturing businesses reported using AI in the Census survey of April 2026.[^41][^20] Hiring runs ahead, with about 11% of manufacturing job postings asking for AI skills.[^23]

faq.q: Will AI take jobs on the plant floor?
faq.a: No, not so far: the data points to help, not cuts. Among US firms using AI, 95.7% reported no AI-driven change in headcount.[^20] Manufacturers also face up to 1.9 million unfilled jobs by 2033.[^42][^43]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when the process is standard, such as maintenance software, condition monitoring or one camera station, and you have no data team. Most firms now buy: 76% of enterprise AI use cases are purchased.[^44] Bought or partnered tools succeed about 67% of the time, three times the rate of internal builds (self-reported).[^45]
buyVsBuild.build: Build, or configure, when your edge is your own data: an assistant over your manuals and repair history, or scheduling on your routings.[^4][^18] Custom industrial AI may need data scientists on staff or a specialist.[^13] Check claims hard: Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by 2027.[^46]

pickElse: Preventive work keeps slipping: fix the basics with maintenance software (a CMMS) and a schedule before predictive AI. NIST's big gap is reactive versus planned work, and MaintainX and Fiix have free tiers.[^1][^25][^26]

The check is simple and stable, like presence, a size or a color: use rule-based machine vision, not deep learning. NIST MEP says rule-based tools are simpler, stable and suit parts with defined criteria.[^13]
Escapes are rare and cheap: skip the camera. NIST MEP says to cost the problem first and weigh a simple fix against AI.[^14][^13]

The process is stable and the problem is variation: use statistical process control (SPC) or lean before machine learning. SPC flags output that falls outside limits set from your own past data.[^51][^13]

offer.heading: Which machine or defect should you point AI at first?
offer.body: Point AI first at the machine whose stops cost you the most downtime, or the defect that most often reaches customers. Bring that one to a free 30-minute call and leave with the first job to fix and the number to measure. No slides and no sales pitch.

reviews.notes: Would distrust a ranked list with no sense of how long the first job takes. Fixed: the troubleshooting-assistant entry now says one plant built it in two weeks and cut repair time 40% (McKinsey). Payoff measures per job are usable as is; own-data method and limits are stated under the table.

On a 390px phone the tool table's 'What it does' cells and two rule statuses were too long to scan. Fixed: cut each tool cell to a few words and shortened the CMMC and NIST SP 800-82 statuses. Also defined ERP on first use. CMMS, OT, SBOM, SPC and CUI are defined where they first appear.

Wants to know one site or line can pilot it and what it does to the unit. Fixed: offer now promises the first job to fix on one line, with a before-and-after number. Sharpened the first bottom-line bullet from 'the basics' to 'basic maintenance' so it is clear what to fix.

Read as a VP of operations or plant manager. Would close the tab on predictive maintenance without a sensor cost. Fixed: the big-company FAQ now gives software prices per user and says sensor systems are quoted per site, citing the vendors' own pages. Checked the rules list names who each rule applies to (medical devices, defense suppliers, EU sellers).

Steve: the second bottom-line bullet said 'published cases report faster repairs', which reads as hype. Fixed: it now gives one plant's 40% repair-time cut. Added 'No slides and no sales pitch' to the offer to answer the paying-for-slides worry. Prices, data, security and skills worries each have a block; no proof from a firm his size is available, so none is claimed.

answers.human-role: Operators, maintenance planners, quality managers and technicians keep every decision about machines, repairs and what ships. AI only flags, sorts and answers questions.[^10][^12][^16][^4]
answers.ranked: AI pays first as a troubleshooting assistant for maintenance, then as predictive maintenance on the few machines that stop the line, then as camera inspection on one costly defect.[^3][^4][^19][^5]
answers.table-1: Maintenance software with AI features runs from free to $75 per user a month. Sensor-based systems are quoted per site, not published.[^25][^26][^27][^50][^49]
answers.table-2: The studies find that planned maintenance cuts downtime and defects, but most AI vision never leaves pilot and productivity dips before it gains.[^1][^19][^7][^8]
answers.rules: Every US plant faces OSHA lockout/tagout and machine guarding rules. FDA, defense (CMMC) and EU machinery rules apply only if you make medical devices, defense parts or EU-sold machines.[^11][^29][^16][^32][^34] Voluntary NIST and CISA guidance covers how to oversee and secure AI on the plant floor.[^12][^10]
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI in manufacturing goes wrong when pilots never reach the line, productivity dips during the ramp, false alarms pile up, or vision models drift when parts or lighting change.[^7][^8][^13][^36] Connected machines also draw cyberattacks, and vendors can lock in your data.[^38][^14]
answers.buy-or-build: Buy for standard jobs like maintenance software, condition monitoring or one camera station. Build or configure only where your own manuals, repair history or routings are the edge.[^44][^45][^4]
answers.something-else: Pick something other than AI when preventive work keeps slipping, a check is simple and stable, escapes are rare and cheap, or the problem is plain process variation.[^1][^13][^14][^51] Maintenance software, rule-based machine vision or statistical process control fits those cases better.[^25][^13][^51]
